# Borderline inverse-power Ball-simplex equality is projective radiality
projective changes of variables is asserted to preserve a mixed-integer
lattice or sampled fiber measure.

## 1. Precise classification

Let r>=2 and beta=r+1. Let f be a nonnegative integrable density on R^r,
with positive finite mass and full-dimensional convex positive support.
Assume that g=f^(-1/beta), extended by +infinity off that support, is
convex. Fix an interior point y and translate it to zero. All statements
about values on support boundaries are modulo Lebesgue null sets.
Define the Ball radial body B by

    rho_B(u)^r = r integral_0^infinity t^(r-1)f(tu)dt.

The audited inverse-power Ball theorem applies at beta=r+1. In particular
B is a convex body with zero in its interior, g(0)>0, g is finite and
continuous near zero, and every positive radial support interval has a
finite positive ray integral. Write p_B for the gauge of B.

**Theorem.** Suppose B is a simplex. There exist a linear functional ell,
an endpoint R in (0,infinity], and a positive continuous profile F on
[0,R), such that the following statements hold.

1. h=F^(-1/(r+1)) is convex and nondecreasing on [0,R), and

       r integral_0^R t^(r-1)F(t)dt = 1.                 (1)

2. If R<infinity then R max_B ell<=1. If R=infinity then ell=0.
   Thus 1-ell(b)>0 for every b with p_B(b)<R.

3. The map

       Phi(b)=b/(1-ell(b))                              (2)

   maps {p_B<R} bijectively onto the interior of the support of f.
   Its inverse is Psi(x)=x/(1+ell(x)); the latter denominator is positive
   throughout that support. The density is

       f(x)=(1+ell(x))^(-(r+1))
                    F(p_B(x)/(1+ell(x)))               (3)

   there, and zero outside its closure. Equivalently f(x)dx is the
   pushforward under Phi of F(p_B(b))db.

Conversely, any B containing zero in its interior, any F satisfying the
profile and normalization conditions, and any ell satisfying condition 2
define by (2)--(3) an integrable inverse-power convex density whose Ball
body is B. The necessity of (2)--(3) here is asserted for simplices.

The endpoint may satisfy R max_B ell=1: the transformed support can be
unbounded. No positivity at the endpoint or across a projective pole is
required. Boundary values of F and f do not affect the theorem.

There is also an intrinsic formula for the projective parameter. Put

    L(x)=g'(0;x)/g(0),

where the one-sided directional derivative exists and is finite because
g is convex and finite in a neighborhood of zero. Then

    L(x)=ell(x)+c p_B(x),   c>=0.                        (4)

Thus ell is uniquely determined by g and the actual Ball simplex B.
If v_0,...,v_r are its vertices and sum alpha_i v_i=0 with alpha_i>0
and sum alpha_i=1, then c=sum alpha_i L(v_i).

## 2. Equality of the ray transport on a simplex facet

For x in the boundary of B define its normalized ray distribution and
quantile by

    F_x(t)=r integral_0^t s^(r-1)f(sx)ds,
    R_x(v)=F_x^(-1)(v),              0<v<1.

The inverse is taken before the endpoint of the positive radial support.
There the density is positive and continuous, so R_x is C^1, strictly
increasing, and

    R_x'=g(R_x x)^(r+1)/(r R_x^(r-1)).                  (5)

Take two points x_1,x_2 in one facet and z=lambda x_1+(1-lambda)x_2,
0<lambda<1. All three ray laws have total mass one. At a fixed v put

    T=(lambda/R_1+(1-lambda)/R_2)^(-1),
    a=lambda T/R_1, b=(1-lambda)T/R_2,
    X=g(R_1 x_1), Y=g(R_2 x_2).

Then a+b=1, T=aR_1+bR_2, and Tz=aR_1x_1+bR_2x_2 is in the interior of
the positive support. Differentiation, convexity of g, and weighted
Holder give

    r T^(r-1)f(Tz)T'
      >= T^r [a X^(r+1)/R_1^r+b Y^(r+1)/R_2^r]
                        /(aX+bY)^(r+1)
      >= T^r/(aR_1+bR_2)^r
       = 1.                                             (6)

T is strictly increasing from zero. Its image is contained in the
positive radial interval at z, possibly omitting a final part. Integrating
(6) over v in (0,1) cannot exceed the total ray mass one at z. Hence the
continuous integrand equals one at every v. Both positive inequalities
in (6) are equalities, and there is no omitted positive ray mass. More
particularly integration up to any v gives

    F_z(T(v))=v,   R_z(v)=T(v).                          (7)

The equality condition in Holder is

    X/R_1=Y/R_2.                                        (8)

For completeness, Holder was applied to

    aX+bY = sum_{i=1}^2
             (a_i X_i^(r+1)/R_i^r)^(1/(r+1))
             (a_i R_i)^(r/(r+1)).

Equality, with both weights strictly positive, says X_i^(r+1)/R_i^r
is proportional to R_i, which is exactly (8).

Equation (5) now gives

    (1/R_1-1/R_2)'=0.                                  (9)

No strict-convexity, differentiability of g at zero, or strict exponent
has entered this step.

## 3. Identifying every reciprocal-quantile constant

Write f_0=f(0)>0. On any fixed ray convex differentiability from the
right at zero gives

    g(tx)=g(0)(1+t L(x)+o(t)),
    f(tx)=f_0(1-(r+1)t L(x)+o(t)).

Consequently

    F_x(t)=f_0 t^r(1-r L(x)t+o(t)).

With t_0=(v/f_0)^(1/r), inversion yields

    R_x(v)=t_0+L(x)t_0^2+o(t_0^2),
    1/R_x(v)=1/t_0-L(x)+o(1).                          (10)

Here only the expansion on each fixed ray is used; no uniform directional
Taylor remainder is asserted. Combining (9) with (10), for points on a
common facet,

    1/R_1(v)+L(x_1)=1/R_2(v)+L(x_2).                    (11)

The directional derivative L is finite, continuous, positively
homogeneous, and convex. Formula (7), followed by (10), gives

    L(lambda x_1+(1-lambda)x_2)
             =lambda L(x_1)+(1-lambda)L(x_2).           (12)

Thus L is affine on each facet. All facets of an r-simplex with r>=2
have nonempty pairwise intersections. A shared boundary ray therefore
identifies the functions in (11) on distinct facets. There is a single
function Q(v) such that, for every x in the boundary of B,

    1/R_x(v)+L(x)=Q(v).                                 (13)

Let v_i and alpha_i be as in the theorem. Define c=sum alpha_i L(v_i).
Convexity implies c>=L(0)=0. The values L(v_i)-c have weighted sum zero,
so there is a unique linear functional ell taking those values at the
vertices: this is the usual unique affine interpolation on a simplex,
whose interpolating affine function has value zero at the origin.
On each facet, (12) implies L=ell+c. Positive homogeneity then proves
(4) on every ray. In particular, on the boundary of B, L=ell+c.
Replacing Q by q=Q-c in (13) gives the exact global identity

    1/R_x(v)=q(v)-ell(x),       x in boundary B.         (14)

The simplex assumption is essential to this deduction: arbitrary values
on the vertices of a general polytope need not have the form ell+c.

## 4. The global positive chart and radial transformed density

For every v and every boundary point x, R_x(v) is positive and finite.
Taking a point maximizing ell on B in (14) shows

    q(v)>max_B ell>=0.                                  (15)

The second inequality holds since zero is interior to B. If ell is
nonzero, the maximum is strictly positive. If ell=0, (14) also gives
q(v)>0. Differentiating (14) at any fixed boundary point gives q'(v)<0.
By (10), q(v) tends to infinity as v decreases to zero. Put

    rho(v)=1/q(v),     R=lim_{v increases to 1} rho(v).

Then rho is C^1 and strictly increasing from zero onto (0,R).
Equation (15) implies R max_B ell<=1 if R is finite, and forces ell=0
if R is infinite. The possible equality at the endpoint does not affect
strict positivity in the open set {p_B<R}.

Every point in the interior support is t x with x on the boundary of B
and t=R_x(v) for a unique v. By (14),

    1+t ell(x)=t q(v)>0,
    Psi(tx)=rho(v)x.                                   (16)

This proves both that Psi is defined throughout the support and that its
image is exactly {p_B<R}. Its inverse is (2). In particular no extra
component of support lies across a pole. The original interior support
is exactly

    {x: 1+ell(x)>0, p_B(x)<R(1+ell(x))},                (17)

with the infinite-R case interpreted as all of R^r (ell=0).

The derivative of Phi has determinant

    det D Phi(b)=(1-ell(b))^(-(r+1)).                   (18)

One can obtain this by the determinant formula for a rank-one update,
or by choosing a basis in which ell is a coordinate functional; for
ell=0 it is immediate. Hence the transformed density and its convex
potential are

    f_tilde(b)=f(Phi(b))/(1-ell(b))^(r+1),
    g_tilde(b)=(1-ell(b))g(Phi(b)).                      (19)

The latter is convex on the positive chart. Indeed, for b=theta b_1+
(1-theta)b_2 put d_i=1-ell(b_i)>0 and d=theta d_1+(1-theta)d_2.
Then Phi(b)=(theta d_1/d)Phi(b_1)+((1-theta)d_2/d)Phi(b_2).
Convexity of g, multiplied by d, is exactly convexity of g_tilde.

For points x_1,x_2 in one facet, equations (8), (14), and (16) show

    g_tilde(rho(v)x_i)
        =rho(v) g(R_{x_i}(v)x_i)/R_{x_i}(v),

which is independent of i. Facet intersections again identify all these
values. Thus g_tilde(b)=h(p_B(b)) on {p_B<R}, for a positive continuous
h. Restriction to any ray makes h convex. It is also nondecreasing:
for 0<=s<t<R, a point of sB is a convex combination of vertices of tB,
all of which have g_tilde value h(t); hence h(s)<=h(t).

Putting F=h^(-(r+1)) proves (3). Change of variables (18) preserves the
finite positive total mass. Along any fixed boundary ray, with
t=rho/(1-rho ell(x)), its radial integrand transforms exactly as

    t^(r-1)f(tx)dt = rho^(r-1)F(rho) d rho.             (20)

The original Ball normalization gives (1). All arguments hold on support
interiors. The boundary of a full-dimensional convex set is Lebesgue
null, including for an unbounded support, so no assertion about endpoint
values was silently needed.

## 5. Converse, including support that reaches a pole

Let B, R, F, ell satisfy the displayed conditions in the theorem. The
open domain V={p_B<R} lies in {1-ell>0}. Formula (2) is a bijective
projective map from V to (17). For finite R the latter set is convex
because p_B(x)-R ell(x)<R is a convex strict sublevel condition and
implies 1+ell(x)>0. For infinite R, ell=0 and there is no transformation.

The density in (3) is the pushforward of F(p_B), by (18). Polar
integration and (1) give its mass |B|, hence integrability even when the
image is unbounded. The potential on that image is

    g(x)=(1+ell(x))h(p_B(x)/(1+ell(x))).                 (21)

The same convex-perspective argument as in Section 4, now applied to
the convex function b->h(p_B(b)), proves convexity of (21) on its
convex support. Extending it by +infinity off the open support remains
convex; boundary values may instead be chosen by any convex extension
without changing the density measure. Finally (20) proves that its
Ball radial body is exactly B. This proves the converse.

## 6. Ordinary minimum-maximal-depth corollary

Under the stated full-dimensional inverse-power assumptions, the audited
ordinary inverse-power depth theorem gives D(f)>=Gamma_r, attained at an
interior point, with a finite cover by active through-center halfspaces.
The audited ordinary simplex rigidity theorem then implies that
D(f)=Gamma_r only if its Ball body at a deepest point is a simplex with
centroid zero: through-center cap fractions are preserved by the Ball
construction, and the active caps cover the entire ambient space. The
present theorem therefore gives the following exact borderline equality
classification for r>=2:

    D(f)=Gamma_r if and only if, about some interior point,
    f is a positive-chart projective image (2)--(3) of an integrable
    gauge profile on a centroid-centered simplex, with the convexity,
    endpoint, and normalization conditions above (or their rescaled
    unnormalized equivalent).

Here sufficiency needs no new rigidity argument. Every gauge profile on
a centroid-centered simplex has depth Gamma_r at zero; its canonical
vertex caps through zero cover the whole space and each has that mass
fraction. Projective changes within a positive chart preserve halfspace
depth exactly. Explicitly, the preimage of a halfspace {a.x>=b} is, on
V,

    {(a+b ell).b_variable>=b}.

The inverse rule is obtained with the opposite sign. Thus halfspace
intersections with the two supports correspond in both directions. If
a transformed normal happens to be zero, its intersection is either
empty or the whole support, and this also is represented by an ordinary
halfspace on that support, or contributes the trivial mass zero/one.
At a candidate in the open support the containing empty case is
impossible. Candidates outside the closure of the convex support have
depth zero by separation; candidates on its boundary have depth zero
because a supporting hyperplane has density measure zero. Consequently
no candidates omitted by the positive chart can increase the maximum.

Dimension one is excluded: its two boundary points belong to disjoint
zero-dimensional facets and the ray-equality argument is unavailable.
This source does not classify a borderline density with a nonsimplex
polyhedral Ball body and makes no mixed-integer claim.

## 7. Dependencies and audit scope

The analytic Ball bounds, convexity of its radial body, and ordinary
inverse-power depth theorem are proved in
`candidate 2338b9b22d6faa2f` and
`candidate 55fd8fec61360536`. The ordinary
simplex rigidity dependency is
`candidate e2c55c91458e1e8c`.
Sections 2--5 supply the new borderline equality proof; Section 6 invokes
only those already audited ordinary results. The strict-exponent sibling
is `candidate 07f233a26b321ff2`.

## 8. An exact calibration with a boundary pole

Take the centroid-zero triangle B with vertices (1,0), (0,1), (-1,-1).
Its gauge is

    p_B(x,y)=max{x+y,x-2y,-2x+y}.

Let R=1, ell(x,y)=x, and F(t)=4/(1+t)^3 for 0<=t<1. The normalization
is exact, since 2 integral_0^1 t F(t)dt=1. Now max_B ell=1, so the
radial support touches the pole at (1,0). Its projective image is the
unbounded convex set

    -1/2<y<1,   x>(y-1)/3.

The classified density on this set is

    f(x,y)=4/[1+x+p_B(x,y)]^3.

Its inverse cube root is a positive multiple of 1+x+p_B, hence convex.
The density has total mass |B|=3/2, despite its unbounded support.
For a boundary point v of B, write a=ell(v). Its support ray endpoint
is t=1/(1-a) if a<1 and infinity if a=1. Its ray CDF is exactly

    F_v(t)=4 [t/(1+(1+a)t)]^2,

whose endpoint limit is one in both cases. Its quantile satisfies

    1/R_v(w)=2/sqrt(w)-1-a.

This exhibits the common function q(w)=2/sqrt(w)-1, the full pole
endpoint, the unchanged Ball body, and the nonconstant radial profile.
The maximum depth is Gamma_2=4/9 by Section 6. This is solely an ordinary
continuous example.
